Following the election of Donald Trump as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainties. With the new US administration taking office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two areas — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, amid faster US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and the potential adoption of US trade protectionist measures, risks facing emerging market economies have intensified. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have risen in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Nonetheless, liquidity conditions remain sound, and overall loan growth picked up further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment but has rebounded recently. Looking ahead, banks should prudently assess the impact of potentially faster-than-expected US rate hikes and, more broadly, US policy uncertainties, particularly the risk of large capital outflows and the potential implications for local interest rates. Following the election of Donald Trump as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainties. Not only did the election outcome surprise the market, but the associated market reactions were also unexpected. In particular, expectations that Trump’s tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove global stock markets higher. With the new US administration taking office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two areas — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the anticipated Trump tax cuts may not deliver the expected stimulus to US economic growth. Specifically, with US economic activity already near its potential, fiscal stimulus may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US growth but could exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen notably, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" situation for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would distort markets, harm overall welfare, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy, where the recovery remains fragile. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows has increased due to faster US rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation. This could weigh on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration and concerns over surging energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to a broad-based rise in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US rate hike expectations on the sovereign debt markets of 26 selected economies. The findings show that the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign debt markets has deepened since the "taper tantrum" of 2013, and that US rate hikes and tightened financial conditions could have significant impacts on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 alongside a recovery in exports, but market volatility — including currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region due to earlier concerns over potential policy changes by the new US administration — only began to stabilise early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but risks and uncertainties are both elevated. US rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility could lead to tightened financial conditions. Meanwhile, the potential adoption of protectionist policies by the US could affect regional economies, though the actual impact remains unclear. In Mainland China, overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust infrastructure investment growth and improved private sector business spending. While the economy continues to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties surrounding the growth outlook persist. In particular, with the government determined to curb housing price increases, if the property market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate sector to growth may diminish this year. At the same time, ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations could increase short-term uncertainties in the economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US rate hikes, but appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activity, there remain some concerns in the market about the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given the acceleration in M1 growth alongside a slowdown in M2 growth. Box 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) examines factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence of a liquidity trap in the Mainland, and the main reason for M1 growth significantly outpacing M2 growth is the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid money due to monetary easing in recent years, as well as increased economic uncertainties that may have boosted precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. Externally, merchandise export growth improved alongside better regional trade flows, while exports of services grew steadily with the recovery in trade-related and transport services. As imports of goods and services grew faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With the uptick in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2017 at 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong’s external demand. Amid US dollar appreciation pressures and expectations of faster US rate hikes, global financial conditions are expected to become less supportive of the real economy, and could lead to tightened local financial conditions, especially in the event of tail risks. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of a Hong Kong financial conditions index to help monitor local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained broadly stable, though it occasionally weakened after the US rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered. With the US dollar appreciating, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Due to the large Monetary Base, Hong Kong interbank rates remained low, but rose from October onwards due to year-end funding demand and the catch-up with the US rate hike. As a result, the average mortgage rate edged up to 2.07% in January 2017, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the housing loan market. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by stronger local economic activity and increased financing demand from multinational corporations at year-end. Local loan growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a small decline in the first half. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. Banks’ funding positions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio edged down to 77.1% at end-2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar LTD ratio declined notably to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. With the US dollar strengthening, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool (including customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) outstanding) consolidated further alongside other offshore renminbi markets, and volatility in CNH HIBOR increased significantly. Nonetheless, banks’ renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is likely to continue facing headwinds from uncertainties in the renminbi exchange rate trend. With improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong equity market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected outcome, the market was only briefly impacted. This was mainly driven by investors’ optimism about fiscal stimulus under the Trump administration, which boosted global stock markets. While benefiting from this, the local market was also cautious, possibly due to concerns over faster US rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland’s economic outlook, uncertainties in renminbi policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply at the end of last year and the spread with US Treasury yields widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar debt market expanded steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, but new bond issuance for the full year was still lower than the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi debt markets could come under pressure. Given the uncertainties surrounding US trade policy and the potential for continued renminbi exchange rate volatility, the outlook for these two debt markets over the next six months remains clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the government’s introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment but has rebounded recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined in the following two months. However, transaction volumes have picked up recently, partly reflecting an increase in primary market launches by developers. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, albeit at a slower pace.

Following the unexpected election of President Trump, policy uncertainty in the United States has increased. Although market attention has focused on the short-term benefits of potentially large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is now close to its potential. Fiscal stimulus may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but it would further exacerbate upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks facing emerging market economies are increasing amid capital outflow pressures from faster US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with recent export volumes also increasing. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, with downside risks to economic growth rising. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved business spending in the private sector. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. Amid the government's determination to curb housing price rises, if the property market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate sector to economic growth may also decrease this year. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 alongside a stronger US dollar and US interest rate hikes, but appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following the unexpected election of President Trump, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as markets anticipated that Trump's policies, such as tax reform, large-scale infrastructure spending, and deregulation, would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating a rally in major stock markets (Chart 2.1). Consequently, market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes heated up, leading to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies However, the anticipated Trump tax cuts may not have the positive impact on US economic growth that markets expect. While a shift in economic policy towards fiscal easing would help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, it is debatable whether now is the right time to implement fiscal easing. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Fed's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, indicating that US economic activity is close to its potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, where the fiscal multiplier is lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital could lead to lower tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with spare capacity diminishing, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on growth is limited, could push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, and potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. Even as upside risks to US inflation increase, the Fed remains cautious about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have already risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market expectations for the future federal funds rate have been revised up to near the Fed's median projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Fed's long-term projections (Chart 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger a risk of significant market volatility. While financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures driving stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US Treasury debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises and adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall welfare, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate projections: Fed vs. market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and drag on the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Euro area is gradually improving, with real GDP growing modestly by 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the Euro area is still only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels compared to the stronger recovery in the US (Chart 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, markets have been concerned about the eventual breakup of the Euro area. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilised after forming a new government and implementing measures to rescue its banking sector, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to rise, and corporate bond spreads have also widened, particularly in peripheral countries, which could create a vicious cycle for the real economy and potentially weigh on business real investment in the Euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies In Japan, real GDP has been revised upward in recent quarters, with the annualised growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 increasing to 1.6% year-on-year, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected economic recovery. However, partly due to structural problems in the labour market, wage growth has been slow, leading to weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent sharp depreciation of the yen suggests that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation from the earlier yen appreciation is about to begin to fade. Combined with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this points to an improvement in the near-term inflation outlook, and "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy), which fell to 0.1% in December, is expected to bottom out and recover. That said, amid long-standing and structural headwinds, growth may remain sluggish, and inflation expectations remain around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the level at the launch of Abenomics in early 2014, so the risk of inflation failing to reach the Bank of Japan's 2% medium-term target persists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth through trade channels may be smaller, given the decline in US imports since the global financial crisis and the potential for US protectionist policies. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation will lead to tightened financial conditions, exacerbating downside risks to the economy. This could drag on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration, coupled with concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across both advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP growing modestly and inflation rising. Real GDP growth – In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable as private consumption was steady in several regional economies. At the same time, exports generally edged up from their low levels in 2015. This benefited not only from stabilised growth in China, but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (e.g., Malaysia and Indonesia), the recovery in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained momentum, driven by growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation – With the recovery in commodity prices, especially oil, producer price inflation generally showed an upward trend. While this will push up industrial costs or even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may improve due to reduced risks of prolonged deflation. Faster producer price inflation could put upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumer price index suggest that inflation in several regional economies, while still slightly below central banks' 2017 inflation targets, will rise closer to target levels (Chart 2.4). Except for Indonesia, central banks in East Asia generally maintained an accommodative monetary policy stance, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline consumer price index inflation, forecasts, and central bank targets in East Asia Despite improvements in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 led to short-term financial market volatility. Foreign exchange market – Following the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated less or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Spot foreign exchange depreciation against the US dollar and changes in nominal effective exchange rates after the US election Bond and equity markets – Asset prices briefly fell after the US presidential election but quickly stabilised. Sovereign bond spreads over US Treasury bonds in East Asian economies widened. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined but have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed from pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads of 10-year sovereign bonds over US Treasury bonds Portfolio investment flows – Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. In the first few weeks of 2017, inflows resumed, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain stable, but at a pace still below historical averages. Financial markets are likely to remain volatile due to heightened uncertainty about US government policies and the Fed's possible policy response. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields could attract capital flows from the region to the US, leading investors to reduce holdings of regional assets, particularly those with already high valuations. Tightened financial conditions in this scenario would also put repayment pressure on firms with large US dollar-denominated debt. At the macro level, a general rise in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, not only dragging on aggregate demand in the short term but also potentially affecting potential growth in the long term. Finally, export-oriented countries in the region face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies from the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has been widening in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, clothing, and textiles. Over the past two decades, as US imports in these industries increased, there has been a significant loss of jobs. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to the region's export-oriented countries.

Private consumption growth accelerated and public-sector building and construction activities were buoyant, leading to a slight pickup in Hong Kong’s economic growth in the second half of 2016. Amid increasing uncertainties in the external environment, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. On a seasonally adjusted basis, real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and robust labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the Hong Kong International Airport Third Runway, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, weak corporate capital spending narrowed the contribution of aggregate investment spending to GDP growth. Externally, both merchandise exports and imports accelerated in tandem with the rise in regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). Trade-related and transport services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters, then edged down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major industries declined in the second half of the year, including retail, accommodation and food services, partly due to a stabilisation of the slowdown in the retail sector. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. Externally, amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate. Coupled with the strengthening of the US dollar, which has led to a rise in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong’s export performance will be dampened. Domestically, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, weighed down by rising interest rates. With an increase in housing supply and the launch of several infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital spending. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% for 2017, while private-sector analysts’ forecasts average 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly from the external environment. Policy uncertainties under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with possible protectionist trade policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The process of the UK’s exit from the European Union and elections in several major European countries may also trigger asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. In addition, US interest rate normalisation will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation has remained generally moderate, despite a pickup in quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index was stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before easing slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly driven by increases in prices of tradable goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic food and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index rose, driven by a narrowing decline in private housing rentals and an increase in public housing rentals in September 2016, but subsequently eased slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rental In the near term, with weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Imported inflation will remain low, as the strength of the Hong Kong dollar partly offsets the impact of a rebound in global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap is estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help ease business cost pressures and thereby dampen inflation in the services component. Despite a tight labour market, wage increases have been modest in recent quarters, with real per capita wages rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 and then falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of persistent external uncertainties leading to cautious business sentiment, labour cost increases should be contained. Furthermore, given the lacklustre retail sales performance in recent months, retail property rental increases are expected to be moderate. Moreover, the impact of earlier softening in private housing rentals will gradually emerge, also helping to ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for 2017 as a whole is expected to decline, with the Government forecasting a full-year underlying inflation rate of 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real per capita wages The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the US accelerates under the Trump administration, it could lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, which may push up local mortgage rates and increase downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar could keep import prices weak and also reduce Hong Kong’s attractiveness to inbound tourists. On the upside, if global economic expansion is faster than expected, it could accelerate Hong Kong’s economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the upward adjustment of the statutory minimum wage, effective from 1 May 2017, could further increase inflation, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Overall loan growth continued to be moderate, partly due to an improvement in the local economic environment. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar fund-flow volatility may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, uncertainties over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to a broad decline in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar stayed steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13-14 December 2016 fuelled market expectations of faster US rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. At the beginning of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening from mid-February as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund-flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators Along with the strength of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). With the effect of narrowing inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners being mild, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) closely tracked the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest Balance of Payments (BoP) statistics showed that non-resident portfolio investment in equities and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and substantial initial public offering (IPO) activities (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, resident portfolio investment in debt securities recorded sizeable outflows, which more than offset the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds showed that portfolio investment outflows occurred in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US rate hikes, put pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicated that Hong Kong portfolio investment came under inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to improved global financial market performance as investors became optimistic about expansionary fiscal policies in the US. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar fund-flow volatility may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. At the same time, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the UK's exit from the European Union (Brexit) process, and elections in EU member states could increase fund-flow volatility. Additionally, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets could put upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar fund inflows. Although northbound trading volumes exceeded southbound volumes in the initial period after the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, rising by a further 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total outstanding amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained broadly stable at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within this, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding EFBNs rose correspondingly, due to the additional issuance of HK$49 billion in EFBNs to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base With the local economy becoming more robust, the growth of Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) quickened from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand from stronger local economic activities and a rebound in IPO activities. Analysed by counterpart assets, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected an increase in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money created by credit expansion and net Hong Kong dollar fund inflows from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a higher growth of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, the growth of total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) rose to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with full-year growth at 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale cost of funding rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained low, they rose partly driven by year-end funding demand and catching up with the increase in US dollar interbank rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half, to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward in line with the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at end-December. Moving into early 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as funding demand eased, while long-term Hong Kong Government Bond yields also edged down in line with US government bond yields. Chart 4.8 HIBORs and 10-year Government Bond yield With the banking system's large deposit base, the increase in retail interest rates was relatively modest. Banks' average cost of funding, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, rising by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). As the cost of funding was relatively stable and competition in the mortgage loan business intensified, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017, following the rise in HIBORs. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of increase in local interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of capital outflows, and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, together with the rise in the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate (REER) in line with the US dollar, may reduce the support of local financial conditions for the real economy. Box 4 discusses the construction of a Hong Kong financial conditions index for monitoring local financial conditions. Driven by stronger local economic activities and rising cross-border financing demand, overall loans rose by a further 4.2% in the second half, following a 2.2% increase in the first half (Chart 4.10). With growing economic momentum, local loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2%, as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. For 2016 as a whole, overall loans grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analysed by economic sector, local loan performance was mixed in the second half (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial and finance-related corporates and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, to some extent reflecting strong financing demand driven by better growth prospects in these sectors. Loans to the construction and property development sectors also accelerated, in line with increased private construction activities. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Local loan growth by selected sectors Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, partly reflecting an improved economic environment, personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal purpose loans) rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11), while residential mortgage loan growth accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting brisk residential transactions between July and October. As a result, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt as a percentage of GDP and its components Banks' funding positions remained broadly stable. Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio edged down from 78.2% at end-June 2016 to 77.1% at end-December (Chart 4.13); meanwhile, the overall foreign currency LTD ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at end-December, with the US dollar LTD ratio dropping sharply to 63.8% due to strong US dollar deposit growth. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio Given expectations of rising interest rates and a rapidly changing macro-financial environment, credit growth will be subject to uncertainties in the period ahead. The HKMA's Credit Conditions Outlook Survey indicated that loan demand remained soft in the near term. Amid the appreciation of the US dollar, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi (CNH) exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi (CNY) for most of the latter part of 2016, closing at a year-low of 6.98 against the US dollar at end-2016. The CNH interbank market again came under liquidity tightening pressure in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight CNH HIBOR once surged to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The subsequent rise in CNH funding costs led to the unwinding of short CNH positions, driving a rebound in the CNH exchange rate in early January 2017, with the CNH-CNY spread turning to a premium. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, and liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and three-month CNH HIBORs falling to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at end-February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared with the same period in 2015, driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment charges. The capital position and asset quality of banks also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained healthy. The funding costs of retail banks stayed stable and low, underpinned by a large retail deposit base. However, banks should carefully assess the impact of a potentially faster pace of US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of significant capital outflows and the subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. In addition, given the continued rise in leverage among non-local corporates, a substantial increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong’s banking sector against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% with effect from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 from 0.95% in the same period of 2015 (the red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment charges. For 2016 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose to 1.10% from 1.05% in 2015. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Wholesale funding costs in Hong Kong rose notably following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose significantly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates However, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained modest. This was because retail deposits were the primary funding source for retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low despite the rate hike. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016, after staying at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. More broadly, the total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar picture. While the average non-deposit market Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, at only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 17 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenors of licensed banks The rise in HIBORs was larger and faster than the increase in banks’ funding costs, which could benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgage loans in recent years, and the rise in interest rates on such loans may help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins could be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there were signs that some banks had reduced their mortgage rate spreads relative to the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the longer term, as the US further raises interest rates, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, which would affect their funding costs and have a more significant impact on net interest margins. The capitalisation of banks remained strong and well above international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stayed at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework, Basel III, which came into effect on 1 January 2013. As such, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data as at December 2012. The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the reporting period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions, although edging down to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016, remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios stayed well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities rose to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks As the growth in total loans and advances and total deposits of retail banks was broadly similar during the reporting period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). The Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency LTD ratios also remained broadly unchanged during the same period. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of retail banks Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks increased slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates show that under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.9). However, given that the pace of US interest rate normalisation may be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the implications of this for their interest rate risk management. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks’ loan portfolios remained sound, with the gross classified loan ratio (CLR) and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans staying at low levels of 0.72% and 0.53% respectively at the end of December 2016. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although the current asset quality remains sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to pay attention to the external environment; as the assessment in Box 5 shows, the banking sector’s loans for use outside Hong Kong have recorded rapid growth since the global financial crisis, reflecting that banks’ asset quality is more susceptible to external factors. Banks’ expectations for short-term credit growth were mixed. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016 showed that, although the majority of surveyed AIs expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the proportion of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk of unsecured personal loans remained contained, with the year-to-date annualised credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of new mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt servicing index for new mortgages 47 rose to 48.8 in the fourth quarter from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average amount of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). The continued normalisation of US interest rates could further increase the personal debt burden. A sensitivity test shows that, if interest rates rise by 300 basis points while other conditions remain unchanged, the index could rise significantly to 67.3 within four quarters. 48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risk of a continued increase in the personal debt burden. Chart 5.12 Average loan-to-value ratio of new mortgages and personal debt burden Chart 5.13 New mortgage loans of surveyed AIs The pace of US interest rate hikes remains a key factor affecting the credit risk of corporate loans. However, the actual impact on the asset quality of individual banks will depend on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of non-financial corporates listed in Hong Kong found that the trends in leverage ratios for local and non-local corporates have shown significant divergence since the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates being more susceptible to debt servicing problems. 50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes on the credit risk of their non-local corporate exposures. Specifically, corporate leverage, as measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio, has risen since the global financial crisis, and this increase was primarily driven by non-local corporates. The leverage ratio of non-local corporates rose to 85% in the first half of 2016 (the red line in Chart 5.14), while the leverage ratio of local corporates remained broadly stable. Global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year as the market reassessed inflation risks in the US. In February, global stock markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, completely reversing the significant gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global stock markets over the past two years with low volatility was underpinned by market expectations of a continuation of the ideal environment of robust economic growth, low inflation and low interest rates. However, these expectations are now facing risks from tightened global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall loan growth continued, albeit at a slower pace. After a modest slowdown in the middle of the year, both the pace of property price increases and transaction volumes picked up in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in capital flows to and from Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant about the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, in view of the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of a larger-than-expected increase in interest rates. After the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) had lingered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global stock markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point falling more than 10%, completely reversing the significant gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was triggered by signs that the global economic recovery could put upward pressure on US wages and prices, which had been low for a long time, potentially leading the US Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global stock markets over the past two years was built on market expectations of a continued ideal economic environment. In the second half of 2017, the momentum of global economic growth continued to strengthen, with economic activities in both advanced and emerging market economies picking up simultaneously. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package, which included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax codes, fuelling market expectations that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the strengthening activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained benign, further reinforcing market expectations of a prolonged period of low global interest rates. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with the US stock market, in particular, repeatedly hitting new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global stock markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightened global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, with the economy now at its output potential, the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts could accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the US Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more quickly. At the same time, as tax cuts will lead to a higher fiscal deficit, the US may issue more government debt in the future, which is expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields at a time when the US Federal Reserve continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation. Outside the US, the strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led to market expectations that their central banks may scale back quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a pall over the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to protect domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These actions have raised concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given these uncertainties in the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the currently high valuations in global asset markets is questionable. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expected rise in the fiscal deficit due to US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); coupled with the expected increase in term premiums from the US Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation, long-term interest rates could be pushed higher, which would be detrimental to asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies are also in an ideal environment of robust growth and benign inflation. With the strong economic performance and optimistic outlook, capital inflows have accelerated, and financial markets have risen in tandem. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from a number of factors: the tightening of global liquidity due to the synchronised normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks; the inward-looking trade policy of the US government; geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporations repatriate large profits to the US in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the US tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with sectors and economies with higher leverage levels being most vulnerable to the impact of tightened financial conditions. In Mainland China, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure investment and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year, the Mainland Chinese economy performed well in the second half of 2017. At the same time, signs of the emergence of the "new economy" have become more apparent, with industries such as high value-added manufacturing and services showing strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from the further advancement of structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt an active fiscal policy stance, which could help mitigate adverse economic changes if necessary. During the review period, progress was made in structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, with the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland's real estate market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks' risk exposure to enterprises in overcapacity industries remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed down in the context of financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints on state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capability appear to have tightened, possibly due to reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, with the stabilisation of the economic situation and reduced risks, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real gross domestic product grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Aggregate investment also rebounded, driven by an increase in corporate capital spending. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods remained a drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports are expected to continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government's and the market consensus forecast for real GDP growth in 2018 are 3 to 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to a number of uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the economic performance of Mainland China under tightened financial conditions, and the trend of the local asset market. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained under control. However, there are signs of a slight uptick in quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum in recent months, with prices of both traded goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up slightly to a still moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect from the rise in newly signed private housing rentals. Affected by funding demand from IPO activities and seasonal funding needs, liquidity conditions tightened, and short covering of the Hong Kong dollar increased, leading to a strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate from September to November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017 onwards. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets, particularly the stock market, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates came under upward pressure from September to December 2017. This was mainly due to funding demand from IPO activities and banks' cautious liquidity management towards the year-end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs were 0.25% and 1.26%, respectively, up 14 and 50 basis points from six months earlier. After easing slightly in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable, unaffected by the recent global financial market correction. Despite intense competition in the mortgage loan business, the average lending rate for new mortgages at banks followed the uptrend in short-term HIBORs, rising to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, the cost of funding for retail banks, after a brief spike in October due to IPO activities, remained generally low, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, with the continued normalisation of US monetary policy, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; if there is a sharp shift in global financial market sentiment, the volatility of capital flows could increase. For the full year of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. After strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth moderated to 5.3% in the second half. The growth rate of both local loans for most industries and loans for use outside Hong Kong declined. The growth of foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to higher US dollar funding costs. In contrast, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth, supported by the favourable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at the end of the year, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to the relatively slow growth of foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the end of the year. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation from September to November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (including total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit), after a slight decline in the first half of the year, picked up slightly in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations for the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decrease, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong picked up in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronous strengthening of the global economy that began in late 2016 has not abated. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets higher through 2017 and into early 2018. However, a sell-off and sharp volatility in global equity markets in February, triggered by a reassessment of US inflation risks, marked an end to the two-year period of calm in financial markets. Looking ahead, risks of tightened global financial conditions and a range of policy and event risks will continue to cloud the global outlook. Against a tight labour market, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Fed continues to normalise its balance sheet, increased issuance of US Treasury securities to finance the tax cuts could add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces multiple downside risks, such as a potentially greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. The materialisation of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face the multiple challenges of guarding against risks to economic growth while also limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, depending in part on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term growth pressures from further structural reforms. With the economic situation stabilising and risks diminishing, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. Riding on the increasingly entrenched cyclical improvement in economic momentum since late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the US saw solid increases in investment and exports, driven by improved private sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also experienced broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilising global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of tax reform in the US, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. Given the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP Growth Projections With growth momentum strengthening in the Euro area and Japan, market expectations of a narrowing divergence in global monetary policy, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, spurred a rise in risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite the Fed raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to normalise its balance sheet, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks' targets, leading markets to expect global interest rates to remain low until recently (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise through 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 hitting repeated record highs, pushing its cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest since the "tech bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies However, since the second half of 2017, concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation caused US long-term Treasury yields to rise steadily, raising questions about the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. Following the release of US data showing higher-than-expected average hourly earnings growth for January 2018, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 fell more than 10% from its peak on 26 January, completely erasing its significant gains for the year, and continued to come under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protectionist measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the CBOE Volatility Index spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking an end to the two-year period of persistently narrow trading ranges (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields, and the potential for monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby clouding the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The key measures in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision designed to reduce the incentive for US companies to park their overseas earnings abroad. While it is not yet certain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output beyond its potential, leading to an overheating economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, it could prompt the Fed to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. Currently, the path of the federal funds rate anticipated by financial markets is more gradual than the projections published by the Fed. However, should inflation surprise on the upside, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Projections Second, given that the tax reform is likely to worsen the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase in the future. As the Fed continues with its balance sheet normalisation programme, which is expected to lead to a rise in term premiums, the increase in US Treasury issuance could exacerbate upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Furthermore, as market expectations for the passage of the US tax cut package increased, US inflation expectations have been rising since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by over 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting concerns over increased Treasury supply pressure and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectation Rate In addition, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for an extended period as most expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is widely believed to have fallen significantly since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). That said, due to (1) a decline in the national saving rate expected from higher fiscal deficits, and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate from corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure, the US R* could face upside risks in the future. A rise in R*, together with the expected increase in term premiums from the Fed's balance sheet normalisation, could signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby posing headwinds to asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* Estimated Using the Laubach-Williams Model Third, the strengthening growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back monetary accommodation. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies experienced a broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economy also accelerated its recovery, with real GDP posting its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017.
