Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, the growth rate of money supply generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but only increased slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits remained largely unchanged compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to a reduction in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit rates were raised. An analysis of corresponding assets shows that the slowdown in Hong Kong dollar M3 growth was due to changes in bank capital and reserves (included in "other items net"). Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets Foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. US dollar deposits recorded strong growth of 8.8% in the second half of the year, driven by increased deposits attracted after banks raised their preferential US dollar deposit rates, thus becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew modestly by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% growth in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Although the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposit size remained large, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank interest rates, making them more volatile than longer-term interbank interest rates (Chart 4.7). The three-month and twelve-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than the averages in June. Moving into 2019, as seasonal demand receded, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined. The averages of the three-month and twelve-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking the movement of the US dollar yield curve. Relative to the end of June 2018, the yields on the three-year and ten-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average cost of funding of Hong Kong dollar for retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate increased from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of rising funding costs, following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to their Best Lending Rates. On the other hand, the average lending rate for new mortgages followed the rise in Best Lending Rates, reaching approximately 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trend of US dollar interest rates, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills, which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of intensified Sino-US trade frictions, the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, driven by optimism over the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore renminbi and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates The ongoing Sino-US trade frictions have not yet had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR was mostly below 4% for most of the review period, with occasional increases due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how the progress of Sino-US trade talks will affect liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half of the year, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which recorded growth of 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew at a faster pace than individual customer deposits. However, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit further declined by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively large number of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, retail banks' profits continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on HIBORs and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks rose notably but remained at a low level. Amid an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nonetheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November onwards, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to persistent uncertainties in Sino-US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, an uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact of a further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to a significant increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks further widened to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to attract longer-term stable funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their best lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Reflecting increases in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. At a broader level, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks rose by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenors of licensed banks The cumulative increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in banks' overall funding costs, which may have a positive impact on retail banks' HIBOR-based mortgage loans, which the industry has been actively promoting in recent years. However, the improvement in net interest margin may become more limited in the future, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached their best lending rate-based cap rates. Given the uncertain timing of future best lending rate increases, the continued upward trend in banks' funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, increased uncertainties in the external environment may cast a shadow over banks' earnings prospects. In particular, against the backdrop of a global economic slowdown, persistent uncertainties in Sino-US trade relations may dampen business sentiment and reduce demand for bank credit. If this leads to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong, well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further rose to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Since 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions have been required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable for 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates that the funding positions of authorized institutions remained stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable for 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a share of total liabilities of all authorized institutions edged up to 55.7% from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at the end of the year (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign-currency LTD ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, as Hong Kong dollar deposit growth was much lower than Hong Kong dollar loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at the end of the year. Nonetheless, given the uncertain pace of further US rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainties in Sino-US trade conflicts, tightening global financial liquidity, and a global economic slowdown, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November 2018 onwards. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was attributable to a slowdown in the growth of domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a decline in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, total loan growth slowed significantly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain subdued in the near term. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2018 showed that among all surveyed authorized institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged in the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Although total loans declined slightly in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio (CLR) and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40% at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio declined slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of retail banks' Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage was expanded to include retail banks' major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed to 3.9% in the second half of 2018 from 5.3% in the first half. This was mainly due to a slowdown in the growth of personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal purpose loans), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal GDP grew more slowly than personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up to 71.9% in the fourth quarter from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that are different from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic impact of the pandemic, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and local environment, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing modestly, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, loan growth slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has broadly softened since mid-2019, albeit with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should carefully assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios under the potential exacerbation of these risk factors. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth initially showed signs of stabilisation, benefiting from increased monetary easing by major central banks, easing Sino-US trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a "no-deal Brexit". However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has sparked market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have sharply cut interest rates and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, with credit spreads widening and stock markets plunging, global financial conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will hit global economic activity, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the pandemic. In the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may become tense again, and trade negotiations between the UK and the EU after Brexit may also prove difficult. Weak global demand continues to drag on economic growth in the East Asia region. Exports from the East Asia region to major destinations such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. While some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region have recently reported revenue growth, it remains to be seen whether the technology product cycle has broadly rebounded. Financial markets reacted positively to the announcement of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US in December 2019, with the trade truce somewhat reducing global trade uncertainties. Nonetheless, the East Asia region will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region's economy may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region could hit Asian tourism, especially those economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Given the close supply chain links with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement with the US has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain due to the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 prioritised economic stability for 2020, while also focusing on controlling financial risks. The latest consensus forecast suggests that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private-owned enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, seen as a sign of "private sector retreat". Box 2, using 2018 listed company data to study the drivers of equity changes in Mainland industrial enterprises, found that private-owned enterprises or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "retreat". While the study found that negative profitability was the largest driver, other factors, especially structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Box 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real gross domestic product (real GDP) declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely impacted consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook, which in turn dampened consumer and business sentiment. With the re-escalation of Sino-US trade frictions, the global economic slowdown, and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The economic outlook for 2020 is expected to be very challenging, and the recent pandemic has also brought significant downside risks. As industries such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transport have yet to recover from the damage caused by social incidents, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and a 100% government-guaranteed preferential low-interest loan for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the pandemic. Analysed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the global economic slowdown, Sino-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further. Box 3 will explore in more detail the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually slowed. Due to the weak economic conditions, consolidation in private housing rentals, and modest imported inflation, inflation is expected to moderate in the near term. The market consensus forecast for headline inflation in 2020 ranges from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Supported by increased demand for Hong Kong dollars related to equities (including initial public offerings (IPOs)), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate further strengthened, partly due to active IPO activities and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened near year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued smoothly and orderly during the review period, with no triggering of the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs). The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (HIBORs) have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market attention on future IPO activities affects the three-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the interest rate cap based on the Best Lending Rate, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but due to reductions in the market Best Lending Rate since November, the average lending rate for new mortgages edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing modestly, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of a potential further deterioration of the coronavirus pandemic amid the uncertain external environment. With Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and robust banking system, the HKMA has the capacity, resources, and determination to deal with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market expectations of a Sino-US trade deal led to a strengthening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, but they faced downward pressure from late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the later part of 2019, the offshore renminbi (CNH) generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with the discount briefly widening at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increased to RMB637.4 billion. Other renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with strong growth in renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system for the full year of 2019 remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland's capital account, increased allocation of renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of global coronavirus infections dashed these recovery hopes, deepening investor concerns about a global economic recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand in the second half of 2019 cast a shadow over the outlook for regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector particularly hard hit. On the other hand, the East Asian region continues to face challenges from weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic demand and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has temporarily reduced external uncertainties, downward pressures persist amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing and the impact of the global economic slowdown, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by the authorities will provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, growth showed initial signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as some easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections and the subsequent economic shock have sparked market concerns, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays a significant role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities in the Mainland and the drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillover effects, potentially impacting the global economy (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose risks of directly dragging down local economic activities.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All-Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China as a percentage of GDP for selected major advanced economies in 2018 In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets continue to face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Beyond the pandemic's development, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, while policy risks have declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, prolonging uncertainties after Brexit. Additionally, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to weak global demand. Exports from East Asia to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are initial signs that the downcycle in the region's technology products is bottoming out, including reports of improved earnings from some major regional electronics companies at the end of 2019,6 it remains to be seen whether a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports will materialise. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, central banks in Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea cut their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after reductions in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand cut its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Due to travel restrictions imposed by many regional economies on Mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit first and hardest, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more affected by the outbreak (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified pandemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese tourists In the near term, the pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects may be temporary, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations point to a near-term deterioration in corporate earnings (Chart 2.8), loose global monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Consequently, regional equity markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of benchmark stock index constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for the private sector in the region to service debt. While lower local interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as discussed in Box 1, the risk of private sector debt overhang may also increase when more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, although this effect may be limited to companies with stronger financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, on the external front, East Asian economies may face increased risks from the increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress in the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, trade tensions between the two countries persist as fundamental trade issues remain unresolved. The rising net trade surpluses of several regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations, in an effort to circumvent tariffs, may continue to seek alternative supply sources beyond the China-centric supply chain. As of November 2019, the cumulative net trade surplus of nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately US$167 billion. If the net trade surplus with the US continues to widen, these Asian economies could become the next targets of trade disputes; for example, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In light of this, despite the trade truce between China and the US, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Net trade in goods with the US Over the past decade, increased integration of international financial markets has led to a significant rise in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds.8 Index-tracking funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds), but also actively managed funds that benchmark against investment indices.9 By introducing overseas investors that would otherwise not be attracted to or engaged with the relevant economies, these funds help develop the financial markets of emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds diversify the investor base of emerging market economies, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really a free lunch? For passive bond funds, there are concerns that such investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, leading to high corporate leverage.10 Furthermore, some argue that the recent growth of index-tracking funds has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This Box assesses the impact of index-tracking investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to bonds based on the weight of constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage has risen sharply after the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of companies in a major index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as a proxy for their bond investments by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investments raises the long-term (but not short-term) leverage of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The blue solid bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the emerging market economy corporate bond market, the expanded long-term bond investor base resulting from passive bond funds is also beneficial for the development of emerging market economy corporates. We also find that the aforementioned effect is only significant for companies with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with stronger solvency and lower leverage (green solid bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent companies do not appear to fall further into a debt trap due to investments by passive bond funds. In summary, the above research suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investments may not significantly increase the solvency risk of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

Hong Kong’s economy contracted in the second half of 2019 as private consumption weakened, investment spending fell and exports underperformed, entering its first recession since 2009. The economic performance in 2020 is expected to be very challenging, with the recent coronavirus outbreak posing significant downside risks. The economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, Sino-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and the development of local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, but the outlook faces potential upside and downside risks. Hong Kong’s economy contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. Year on year, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018 and the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, leading to a visible contraction in private consumption from the third quarter.33 Amid increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, aggregate investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 Externally, Hong Kong’s external trade performance continued to be sluggish amid intensified Sino-US trade frictions, weaker global economic growth and a sharp drop in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2).35 Net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter due to a sharp contraction in exports of services, but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and sectors severely impacted, such as retail, food services, transport and tourism.36 To provide banks with greater room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HKD 200-300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. The economic performance of Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to be very challenging, with the recent outbreak posing significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by social incidents, the outbreak will deliver a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash handout to adult permanent residents and a 100% government-guaranteed special low-interest loan for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.37 The HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020, allowing banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak amid fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. Externally, the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-boundary economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the growth estimates by international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks as discussed in previous chapters. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate for the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in total employment was mainly from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in light of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to rise further. Box 3 will discuss in more detail the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, inflation momentum gradually moderated. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures on a number of CPI components. For tradeable goods, basic food inflation remained notable due to rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained mild. For services, the growth of the CPI rental component showed a declining trend, in line with the moderation in the growth of newly signed private housing rentals (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up slightly but remained at a moderate level in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, the weak economic conditions and the widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private housing rentals continue to moderate, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, import inflation is expected to remain mild amid weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2020 ranges from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the headline inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (e.g. due to the persistence of the coronavirus outbreak), it could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it would pose upside pressure on inflation. Despite the notable economic slowdown in Hong Kong, the unemployment rate remained at a low of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only with the persistence of social incidents that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this box analyses the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market, including exploring why the overall labour market was broadly stable in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing), and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand involves costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although the Sino-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt a heavy blow to employment in the trade and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economic recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained stable, and financial activities in fintech development and initial public offerings were also very active. These factors may have helped support the labour market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the public administration, social and personal services sectors have a more neutral response to the economic cycle. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected cyclically. Chart B3.2 Change in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in total employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, with the economy contracting visibly in the second half of the year, the decline in total employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although total employment fell during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped mitigate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some structural changes in the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may have helped companies retain staff. In fact, the proportion of self-employed and underemployed persons as a share of total employment has fallen to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group in the total employed population (about 7% in 2017).42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the higher proportion of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October, with the upward momentum further increasing in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. The strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was partly attributable to equity-related demand and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened towards the year-end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Although the uncertain external environment and market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus epidemic may lead to increased fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand capital outflow pressures without compromising its financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including from initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Moving into December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar further increased, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strength of the Hong Kong dollar was partly due to active initial public offering activities and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened towards the year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes Broadly tracking the movements of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small, thus having a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the movement of the REER broadly followed that of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER When assessing fund flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows, which helps assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. The two concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for Hong Kong dollars will naturally decline, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of 7.85 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months, so no significant outflow of Hong Kong dollars was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits with banks in Hong Kong is a useful indicator. When there is a large outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus epidemic on Hong Kong’s monetary environment remains limited. However, the risks arising from the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic need to be closely monitored. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued currency notes and coins, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicator remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and then edged up by 0.2% in the seven-month period since end-June 2019. An analysis of the corresponding assets shows that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and a rise in the Monetary Base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins) (Chart 4.5). In the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in corresponding assets In the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits, measured in Hong Kong dollar terms, recording a slight decrease. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates experienced volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the active initial public offering activities in the Hong Kong equity market. The Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank offered rate experienced greater fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally rose. Large initial public offering subscriptions can put significant pressure on the overnight interbank offered rate. Box 4 uses empirical analysis to show that market attention to future initial public offering activities also affects the three-month Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate. This situation can arise if market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines for large initial public offerings and prepare medium-term funds in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downwards following the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks continuing to raise preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds, leading to a rise in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate at end-October 2019, several retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks are currently in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. For mortgage loans, in the case of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate-based mortgage loans, major banks raised the interest rate cap determined by the Best Lending Rate, so the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.63% in October. 45 With the Best Lending Rates in the market being lowered since November, the average mortgage lending rate subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus epidemic to US economic activity and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates track US dollar interest rates over the long term, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates may be affected by local factors that could influence the demand for Hong Kong dollars, such as initial public offering activities in Hong Kong. The Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, and the sensitivity of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates to changes in the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment and settlement. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. Should there be a short-term liquidity shortage, banks can use the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA for banks. Amid the possibility of intensified trade conflicts between China and the US, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Moving into October, amid market expectations of a resumption of trade negotiations between China and the US, the renminbi’s depreciation trend reversed, and the offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter, briefly breaking through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US. However, since late January, due to the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic, the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, and at a premium for most of the later part of 2019, with the discount briefly widening at end-January 2020, but the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite the volatility in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share adjustment, and around the Lunar New Year holiday at end-January 2020.

Amid increased uncertainties in the global and Hong Kong economic environment, the profit of Hong Kong retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. That said, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although the growth of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the same period in the review period. Correspondingly, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio and Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio of all authorized institutions (AIs) both increased. However, given the stable level of the aggregate balance of the banking system and broadly stable deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and individual debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact of these risk factors, which may intensify, on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks59 recorded a slight decline of 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, loan impairment charges and operating expenses of retail banks both increased, leading to a slight decline in profit. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point cuts in the US federal funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure. On the contrary, affected by various local factors (including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large initial public offerings, and relatively tight interbank market liquidity conditions), short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-term HIBORs remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR staying at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months ago (the blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained near zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted average cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% at the end of 2019, but remained at a low level by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HIBORs, providing support to the banking sector's profit in the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenors of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks required to comply with the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and tenor have been calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cloud banks' profit outlook. These factors include uncertainties related to the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of Sino-US trade relations, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors could further dampen the already weak momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the low global interest rate environment may persist, which could put pressure on banks' net interest margins in the future. On the local front, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies in the future, it could worsen the outlook for credit demand and banks' asset quality. In terms of overall market development, with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) granting eight virtual banking licences, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to roll out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, the long-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate the adoption of fintech applications to maintain competitiveness. The results of Box 5 show that the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profit levels. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above minimum international standards. As at the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs further increased to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratios, the Basel III non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement is designed to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs Measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)65 requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR),66 as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, reflects the stable funding position of AIs. The average NSFR of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity buffers and stable funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all AIs remained broadly unchanged, edging down to 56.3% from 56.4% six months ago (Chart 5.9). Overall, the average all-currency LTD ratio of all AIs rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the year. Given that the aggregate balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have been broadly stable, there were no clear signs of significant outflows of Hong Kong dollars or from the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. We estimate that under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point increase in both Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by the change in total loans and advances of all AIs) recorded a moderate increase of 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was driven by a moderation in the growth of both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the growth rates of 4.5% and 3.5% recorded in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the full year of 2019 rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% recorded for the full year of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hope for economic reopening, boosting global growth prospects. Combined with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies is expected to be uneven. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-term scarring effects of the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers going forward. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system.
