Partly reflecting weak economic activity and lower credit demand due to the recurring pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, but still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, and the banking sector should remain vigilant to the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infection numbers rose. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, which should help the global economy return to normal and accelerate growth. Combined with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. The widespread distribution of vaccines remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn could force central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier, ending financial markets' expectations of "lower for longer" monetary policy. Over the longer term, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including high global debt levels and long-term economic scarring. In East Asia, supported by a recovery in export demand, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and carry trade activities resumed. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces ongoing uncertainties from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with weakening fiscal positions in the region, could sour market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumer activity gradually normalised. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains highly dependent on the development of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecast suggests that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months in early 2020, but then strengthened for the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and the Mainland debt market recorded strong capital inflows. Detailed research shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate volatility (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in domestic demand and further expansion of merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that it contracted for two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector shows that the contraction in consumption and tourism-related sectors was worse than the overall economy under the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help affected industries and citizens, and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme of HK$5,000 and a 100% government-guaranteed special low-interest loan for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to normalise economic activity, the local economy is expected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to many uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which should support Hong Kong's merchandise and service exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while international institutions and private sector analysts forecast average growth of 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. In response to the worsening labour market conditions, the government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund (e.g., one-off grants) to further support industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease in the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation dynamics, has remained at low levels in recent months, albeit with some fluctuations. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be dampened by the slowdown in the growth of newly signed private housing rentals. The market consensus forecast for headline inflation in 2021 is a moderate 1.4%, while the government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund inflows via the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Connects. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HK$263.3 billion flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued in a smooth and orderly manner. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic's development, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand fund-flow volatilities. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance due to the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021. Due to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Following the appreciation of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) also appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to the CNY exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which is still moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, Hong Kong's renminbi bank loans decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border fund flow channels connecting to the Mainland. With the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by a global stock market rally and active buying of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through the Stock Connect, the Hong Kong equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. The global stock market rally was driven by unprecedented monetary easing measures in major economies; optimism about positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period, and briefly broke through the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing significant net outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence quickly recovered as governments around the world launched unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in bond fund inflows into the local market. Despite a modest rebound in bond yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually end and the global economy to accelerate growth going forward. Coupled with expectations of "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of financial markets are disconnected from the still challenging macroeconomic environment, and if the economic recovery is weaker than expected, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (e.g., due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the dilemma of when to withdraw policy support and must address the many legacies of the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cloud the economic recovery in East Asia, where slower-growing emerging market economies in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse current optimism, leading to instability in capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually normalised. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely depending on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Therefore, the government announced it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by economic reopenings, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of COVID-19 infections has risen again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, weakening the global growth momentum once more. At the end of 2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread worldwide, exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use by the end of 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, with the global economy returning to normal and accelerating growth. Another factor supporting the global economic recovery is sustained policy stimulus measures, including major central banks' commitment to "lower for longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund upgraded its global GDP growth forecast for 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF real GDP growth forecasts in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, with stock prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rising, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, the strong performance of financial markets contrasts with the still challenging macroeconomic situation, and this disconnect could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of controlling the pandemic depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the global vaccination rate was still low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) exist to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply is expected to exacerbate the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies. If pandemic control is less than ideal, countries may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Share of population that has received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets is based on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, due to the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have risen (Chart 2.4). If inflation turns out to be stronger than expected in the future, central banks may need to scale back the size of monetary easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater financial market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding future US-China relations. The trend of US-China "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly tough stance of both US political parties towards Mainland China, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in US-China tensions could trigger financial market turmoil in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the dilemma of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing these measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect", these measures are costly in the long run, including fiscal burdens and delays in necessary post-pandemic resource reallocation, such as allowing "zombie companies" whose business models are no longer viable to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must address the many problems left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the problems caused by the rapid increase in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a share of GDP Another legacy issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may lead companies to reduce investment, and workers who have been unemployed for a long time may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was mainly driven by a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand for electronic and technical equipment. At the same time, the most severely affected service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact) continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have flowed back in. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds (Chart 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccination programmes, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly due to portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding about 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainties related to the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope for the region's hard-hit service industries and economies, competition for early batches of vaccines worldwide has raised procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacity. Therefore, slower-growing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden halt in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually picking up, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports also maintained growth, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products) (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the economy, Mainland GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution to GDP growth by demand component Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the economic recovery still depends to some extent on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalised, the service sector continues to face some disruption as several northern provinces experience a resurgence of the pandemic. On the external front, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to new waves of the pandemic in most advanced economies. In addition, US-China tensions are unlikely to ease in the short term, but the earlier signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the concluded Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI) with the EU could help further integrate China with other economies, potentially partially offsetting the adverse impact of US-China decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" prioritises areas such as technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy, aiming for per capita GDP to reach the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment capability of bond-issuing companies appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp increase in defaults on state-owned enterprises bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds in 2020 increased (Chart 2.9). While the rise in state-owned enterprises defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "rigid repayment" of state-owned enterprises to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space for some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly in less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Onshore bond default volume and ratio In the second half of 2020, the cost of funding for corporate issuers increased, especially for some higher-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to the rise in funding costs for lower-rated issuers to some extent, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, housing prices in the Mainland continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply issue that plagued third-tier cities in previous years was largely under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales in third-tier cities amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand picked up and merchandise exports expanded further. With the hope that COVID-19 vaccination would normalise economic activity, the Hong Kong economy is expected to return to growth in 2021 after recording its sharpest contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to many uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the Hong Kong economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that it recorded two consecutive years of decline, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector also show that economic activity in most sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors being worse than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending the decline of the previous five consecutive quarters (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Domestic private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, but consumer confidence remained weak amid the re-imposition of social distancing measures under the third and fourth waves of local outbreaks. With a temporary improvement in business sentiment, overall investment spending also grew in the second half of the year. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance, especially to Mainland China, Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Services trade remained weak as global tourism remained stalled. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting that the recovery in merchandise exports was slower than that in imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports In response to the ongoing pandemic, the government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totalling HK$30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to assist industries and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme of HK$5,000 and a 100% personal loan guarantee scheme for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With the hope that COVID-19 vaccines will normalise economic activity, the Hong Kong economy is expected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to many uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support to Hong Kong's merchandise and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low (Chart 3.3), while government figures show that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average wage index for employees, which reflects labour income, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the deteriorating labour market conditions, the government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund (such as one-off grants) to further support industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell notably to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also remained at a low level in recent months, albeit with some fluctuations. Specifically, price pressures for basic food items moderated, and the cost of eating out fell notably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts during periods of dine-in service restrictions. Price pressures for other tradable goods (such as durable goods) remained mild. On the services side, the rental component of the composite consumer price index remained weak as private housing rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also moderated in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, domestic inflationary pressures should remain mild in the near term. In particular, domestic inflation will continue to be dampened by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly signed private housing rentals. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2021 is a moderate 1.4%, while the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 1% and the headline inflation rate at 1.6% for 2021. With the COVID-19 pandemic ravaging the world, inbound tourism in Hong Kong has rapidly fallen into a slump, raising concerns about the scarring effects of this crisis on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this Box conducts an empirical analysis of the impact of a booming inbound tourism sector on Hong Kong's labour market, thereby exploring the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism in Hong Kong has experienced significant ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals decreased during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Since the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply for one to two individual visits to Hong Kong per year, each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009, allowing eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for a one-year multiple-entry "Individual Visit" visa (multiple-entry permit). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors increased substantially. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure connecting Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs in late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and under the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We argue that the introduction of the IVS in 2003 is akin to a random economic shock, as it was largely exogenous in timing and its introduction was not anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our main analysis data come from population data from the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the catering, retail, hotel and transport sectors. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41-65) in the comparison group before and after the implementation of the IVS. We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom from the IVS on the labour market may change over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to work in tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries was notably significant and persistent, remaining at around 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in the probability of employment compared with the older cohort) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the income of workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that after the implementation of the IVS, the income growth of workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and less educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising income gains (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the income of female and less educated workers These results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and less educated workers. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, which suggest that the strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled workers, improving the robustness of the labour market for lower-skilled segments. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to bust, these worker groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU), with the strong-side CU being triggered multiple times during September and October 2020. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund flows via the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Connects. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and persistent tensions in Sino-US relations may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong’s ample foreign reserves and robust banking system enable it to withstand the pressures arising from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side CU, mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund flows via the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Connects (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, as local stock market sentiment improved and market expectations of rising funding demand near year-end grew. With continued active fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the multiple triggering of the strong-side CU led to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side CU was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the Aggregate Balance to increase from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CU was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no abnormal fund flows observed. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) broadly declined, tracking the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and persistent tensions in Sino-US relations may heighten fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (e.g., IPOs), leading to substantial fund inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. With its ample foreign reserves and robust banking system, Hong Kong is able to withstand fund-flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continued fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight months since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance due to the multiple triggering of the strong-side CU. Meanwhile, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs), remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise notably between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased sharply again, mainly driven by large IPO activities at the end of the month. Overall, in the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of IPO activities at end-January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew modestly by 9.1%. Based on an analysis of corresponding assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly due to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side CU (Chart 4.7). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% during the same period; excluding the impact of IPO activities at end-January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew modestly by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and corresponding assets Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% in the seven-month period since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting US dollar weakness, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% during the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding IPO activities at end-January, total deposits grew modestly by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to various short-term factors (e.g., seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), and should therefore be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Although there were large IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not experience significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the interbank market in Hong Kong continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly followed the movement of the US dollar yield curve, steepening during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages At the retail level, Hong Kong dollar interest rates mainly declined in line with HIBORs. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). With lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also declined from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the LERS, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should continue to stay low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity needs. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient cushion to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates strengthened against the US dollar from end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China compared with the rest of the world and US dollar weakness. Following FTSE Russell’s announcement in late September to include Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index, investment demand further supported renminbi strength. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the CNY exchange rate, averaging a premium of around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained modest by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable during the review period. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity needs near year-end, it mostly stayed below 4% (Chart 4.11). The three-month CNH HIBOR tracked the onshore renminbi interest rate, declining in late December and then rising again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the pace of renminbi deposit growth accelerated, to some extent reflecting renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among the total, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, outstanding CDs decreased by 25.0% during the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong For other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion in the seven-month period since end-June 2020. On the other hand, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow strongly. In the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% compared with the same period a year earlier. Among these transactions, the increase in remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was higher than that from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong’s deep renminbi liquidity pool continues to support a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. For 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

The persistent economic downturn caused by the recurring COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with the prolonged low interest rate environment, led to a further decline in the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks in the second half of 2020, along with a slight deterioration in asset quality. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficulties. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume globally, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of these downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed to 1.01% in the second half of 2020 from 1.63% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.2), leading to a decline in net interest income that outweighed a slight increase in non-interest income, resulting in lower profitability. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining notably from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates More broadly, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost for licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenors of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margins. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of the economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9% during the same period, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also reflected a stable funding position of AIs. The average NSFR of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75% respectively. The ample liquidity buffers and sound funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits continued to be the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2020, the share of customer deposits to all AIs' total liabilities stood at 56.1%, broadly unchanged from the level six months ago (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 The liability structure of all AIs As total deposits of all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all AIs declined to 72.3% at the end of 2020 from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, the average Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio and foreign currency LTD ratio declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively at the end of 2020, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months ago. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks' interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a persistent economic downturn due to the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for 2020 as a whole, the banking sector's total credit still recorded positive growth, albeit with the growth rate slowing notably to 1.2% from 6.7% in 2019. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs decreased by 1.8% in the second half of 2020, after growing by 3.0% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was driven by decreases in both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with increases of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six-month period. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared with the level at the end of June, after decreasing by 2.0% in the first half. Foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half of 2020, after recording a substantial increase of 10.6% in the first half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook on short-term credit demand was slightly more optimistic than six months ago. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the share of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase in the following three months rose to 37%, while the share expecting loan demand to decrease in the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capability of households and corporates, banks' loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also moderated in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio (CLR) of all AIs rose moderately to 0.9% at the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months ago, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs rose to 0.57% at the end of 2020 from 0.49% at the end of June 2020. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Moving into 2022, the global economy showed signs of weakness, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify in various places, especially in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic, and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. If the US Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy significantly, leading to tightened global financial conditions, it would put pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. The recent outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits grew modestly during the review period, with no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, the growth in total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the continued economic recovery, and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation could be faster than expected. These risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness continuing into 2022, due to increased restrictions on people's movement globally caused by the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant, and continued supply bottlenecks constraining production. At the same time, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the United States. More recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, a sharp rise in commodity prices could further exacerbate global inflation threats, while increased financial market volatility could lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties in the global economic outlook. In the near term, if there is a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, the re-imposition of lockdown measures and a worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the US Federal Reserve has turned hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing reducing its balance sheet. If the US Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financial conditions could also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing ability, and disorderly capital outflows could put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. The recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could pose a risk of sustained increases in global commodity prices, exacerbate shortages of industrial supplies, and increase financial market volatility. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the momentum was temporarily slowed by the re-imposition of strict COVID-19 restrictions in some Southeast Asian economies in the third quarter, while the region's tech-exporting economies (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia is widely expected in 2022, the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants of the virus remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and strained public health resources. Second, the accelerated policy normalisation by the US Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and increase currency depreciation pressures; economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to inflation in the region and simultaneously weaken consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalisation decisions of central banks in the region will become more complex. Central banks in some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is affected by corporate environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, due to the persistent downturn in the property market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term. Consequently, the Mainland authorities have made stabilising growth the top priority for this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both decreased in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remains manageable, as Mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, with low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but the pace slowed compared with the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew modestly, supported by merchandise exports and private consumption benefiting from the continued global economic recovery, improved local labour market conditions, and the government's Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, economic growth was 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Moving into 2022, a new wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue to recover for 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are affected by a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. With the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid the new wave of local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local epidemic and the tightening of COVID-19 restrictions will put some pressure on the local labour market (especially industries involving face-to-face contact) in the near term. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to price increases for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term. However, subdued rents and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast expects headline inflation to reach 2.4% in 2022, while the government expects headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% in 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local equity market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak net buying through the southbound Stock Connect and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen with the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy normalisation. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded mostly in the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings range, with trading continuing in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits grew modestly during the review period, with no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Hong Kong's interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. With ample interbank liquidity, HIBORs remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. The offshore renminbi banking business continued to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit reaching RMB1,113.5 billion as at the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi RTGS system rose to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland's capital account, increased demand for renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, supported by Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Stock, Bond, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connects. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict have led to a consolidation in major global equity markets since early January 2022.

The rapid global spread of variant viruses (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, led to a significant slowdown in the global economy in late 2021, with growth momentum remaining weak into 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy stance, exacerbating the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and also adversely affect emerging markets, where the recovery generally lagged. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered global financial market volatility, amplifying some of these risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region's major technology product exporting economies continuing to outperform others. While the Omicron variant is not currently causing a severe disruption to the region's economic recovery, any uncertainties related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the normalisation of US Fed policy could trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies could also weigh on the region's merchandise exports growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, pushes up commodity prices and increases inflation risks, and on the other hand, weakens consumption and increases global economic uncertainty, which will complicate the monetary policy normalisation decisions of regional central banks. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, impacted by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and property market tightening measures. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures from a cooling property market and the Omicron variant outbreak. In view of this, the government has made stabilising growth its top priority this year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain issues (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials like semiconductors) continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major AEs, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China offsetting the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF real GDP growth projections Alongside the global economic slowdown, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major AEs, especially in the US, which has implemented larger policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Furthermore, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices of various commodities, which could exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core consumer price index (CPI) inflation in selected economies (1) Latest data for the US, UK, and Euro area are for January 2022, while the rest are for December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asia" includes Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Asian market economies" includes Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with downside risks predominating, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy response of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared to previous lockdown policies, these looser measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of a large-scale outbreak, the re-imposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which would lead to a renewed deterioration of supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Delivery Times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current high global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk of higher commodity prices from the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia, the lagged pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the potential for earlier sharp rises in global residential property prices to feed into higher rents later, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. Notably, given the largest US inflation increases in decades, the US Fed shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory", and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month to end the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and began discussing reducing the balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests the US Fed may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs, given the Euro area's closer trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine. Against this backdrop, coupled with persistently high global debt levels and asset valuations under prolonged accommodative policies, if inflationary pressures persist and lead the US Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, it could worsen borrowers' debt servicing capacity and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, with the escalation of geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. In the context of a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures.
