Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, South Korea and Singapore, as the region's major exporters of technology products, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the unevenness of the recovery across the region. Additionally, inflationary pressures in several emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index The market generally expects a broad recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, but the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread in the region since late 2021, its economic impact remains milder than previous waves of infection; however, some regional economies with still lagging vaccination rates and tighter public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, the normalisation of US Fed policy could trigger capital outflows and put depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support the economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. On the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in US long-term yields could also spill over to emerging Asian long-term bond yields, exacerbating the risk of adjustment in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the region's goods trade outlook faces uncertainties from a slowdown in major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, and these factors could weaken the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP Fourth, although the region's economies have relatively limited trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed into regional inflation while also weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalisation decisions of regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and higher sensitivity of inflation to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also reminds regional economies of the long-term need to rebuild a more sustainable and resilient growth model to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 studies whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how this sensitivity is influenced by firms' environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Fund outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 event In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the large outflows could be investors taking "first-mover advantage" by redeeming early to avoid bearing the potentially sharply higher redemption costs during market stress. To curb outflows driven by first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds use swing pricing – a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical evidence on whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 event, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. Additionally, this box also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations regarding financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming earlier than other investors, thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. First-mover advantage exists primarily in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, where the costs of subscription and redemption by fund investors (e.g., transaction costs from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund price after the transaction. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expectation of rising redemption costs. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open-ended funds.

Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, driven by sustained growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, recording its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity. The overall economy is expected to maintain its recovery for 2022 as a whole, but the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the epidemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook, which had improved notably in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up in the near term alongside rising import prices, subdued local rentals and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), albeit at a moderated pace compared to the first half. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP expanded by 6.4%, the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, improved labour market conditions and the Government's Consumption Voucher Scheme boosted private consumption. However, overall investment spending declined in the final quarter after a strong rebound in the previous two consecutive quarters. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained robust amid the continued global economic recovery, while services trade remained weak, partly due to the still stagnant inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade was a drag on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volume A new wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme until end-October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing epidemic and a higher base of comparison. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2.0%–3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties and risks as discussed in previous chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (e.g., the Russia-Ukraine situation) have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if Hong Kong resumes quarantine-free travel with Mainland China earlier than expected, it could stimulate local economic growth. With the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by end-2021 (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, but remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data showed renewed pressure on the labour market amid the new wave of local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local epidemic and tightened COVID-19 restrictions will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, especially for sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over a longer horizon, labour market conditions will depend on local epidemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remained mild. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, the price increases for meals out and some energy-related items accelerated alongside the recovery in local demand and rising external prices (Chart 3.5). At the same time, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour cost remained weak, it edged up in recent quarters, partly due to some improvement in real average earnings (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong's import prices Chart 3.6 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals Chart 3.7 Unit labour cost Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term alongside rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the epidemic. However, subdued rentals and mild local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for headline inflation in 2022 is 2.4%, while the Government forecasts headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% in 2022.

Amid risk aversion in the local equity market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. HIBORs continued to stay at low levels due to ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, although uncertainties related to US monetary policy, the pandemic and heightened geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system to withstand the impact of such volatility. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings range, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local equity market (Chart 4.1). Despite a mild rebound in October 2021 on improved market sentiment, the Hong Kong dollar subsequently lost momentum, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through Stock Connect (Chart 4.2) and expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the US Fed turned more hawkish on its monetary policy outlook. During the review period, IPO activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable signs of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (HKEX) Despite the US dollar strengthening during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) remained stable as the renminbi appreciated against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties related to US monetary policy, pandemic developments and heightened geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal functioning of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds (the pace and scale of which will depend on market conditions at the time) could lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system to withstand fund-flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base rose by 1.4% in the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills to meet sustained demand from banks amid ample banking system liquidity, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before discount window operations) decreased correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued currency notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) In the six-month period since end-July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities. It is therefore more appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Despite concerns over US monetary tightening, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels due to ample banking system liquidity (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting expectations of higher funding demand towards year-end, HIBORs edged up in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. Meanwhile, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample banking system liquidity should provide a sufficient cushion in the event of large capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates During the review period, the CNH interbank market continued to function normally. The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late December 2021 due to seasonal liquidity demand near year-end, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR fixings In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. In the six-month period since end-July 2021, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increased by 30.3% to RMB1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in outstanding CDs. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong In the six-month period since July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion for the period between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022 (Chart 4.10), up by 18.3% compared with RMB3,181.0 billion during the same period last year. The deep renminbi liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to support a large amount of renminbi payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system rose to RMB1,522.6 billion from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020. Chart 4.10 Flows of renminbi trade settlement payments Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way Stock, Bond, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connects, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global equity markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and heightened tensions between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong equity market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties over Hong Kong’s pandemic development pushed the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low at end-February. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of local epidemic. Major global equity markets generally continued to rally in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). The global economic recovery, supported by government monetary and fiscal stimulus, and strong corporate earnings underpinned the rally in major global equity markets, although the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global equity markets consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies against rapidly rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and heightened tensions between Russia and Ukraine. In contrast, the Hong Kong equity market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets at end-2021. The Hang Seng Index fluctuated between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at end-2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong equity market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties over Hong Kong’s pandemic development and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low of 22,713 points at end-February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 The Hang Seng Index and The MSCI World Index Equity market implied volatilities fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before easing subsequently. Although the SKEW Index retreated from its historical high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, suggesting that investors were willing to pay more to hedge against downside risks, fearing a correction in the long equity market rally since the pandemic outbreak (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and the S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against a backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong equity market continued to record net inflows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, southbound Stock Connect recorded significant net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of Mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, buying through southbound Stock Connect began to pick up in December 2021, recording a net inflow of HK$98.3 billion by end-February. During the review period, the cumulative net buying amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net equity market fund flows into Hong Kong Chart 4.14 Net flows through equity connectivity schemes After reaching a record high in the first half of 2021, Hong Kong’s primary market slowed in the second half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 IPOs, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), representing a 17.8% decline in total funds raised compared with the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth globally in the IPO market, after Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Initial public offering market in Hong Kong The outlook for the local equity market remains uncertain. Easing of Mainland monetary policy and more secondary listings of US-listed Chinese companies in Hong Kong’s primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong equity market. However, the equity market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainties over the local pandemic development, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profit of Hong Kong retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio increased slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by historical and international standards. The Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by sound capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA extended a number of relief measures to further help the economy through the difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the economic recovery, and together with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation could be faster than expected, both will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% in the second half of 2021 compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly attributable to a decline in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets fell to 0.59% from 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s increased issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) edged up in the final quarter of 2021. However, given the still ample liquidity in the banking system, interbank rates remained at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR edged up by 9 basis points from six months ago to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA’s 2021 Annual Report last year, we are publishing the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system’s resilience to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. Over the past year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA’s core functions. You will learn about our specific measures and efforts in this report, with the following key highlights: Banks face climate risks in their daily operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks’ resilience to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the supervisory process and explored how to leverage technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. Recognising the increasing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we also shared good practices with the industry on how to properly manage these products, thereby promoting banks’ ability to strengthen their climate risk management. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives to address climate risks and promote sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will enhance transparency in the financial market and align green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaged in multiple international organisations to help formulate policies to address climate change and assess its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite a challenging year for the global debt market in 2022, Hong Kong’s green and sustainable debt issuance continued to record strong growth, increasing by 42% to a total issuance volume of USD 80.5 billion, making it the largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia². Issuers included the People’s Government of Shenzhen Municipality and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between Mainland China and the international market. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly USD 16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two “firsts”, including the issuance of the first batch of government green retail bonds totalling HKD 20 billion in May 2022, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at that time. Additionally, we assisted the Government in issuing the first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance marked a milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the debt market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for fostering a well-functioning climate finance ecosystem, and their development relies on the efforts and collaboration of various sectors. To this end, the HKMA, primarily through the Steering Group, collaborates with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions, and the financial industry to advance these elements. In addition to developing the local green classification framework as mentioned above, the Steering Group has also promoted skills training in the industry and improved Hong Kong’s data resources through its Green and Sustainable Finance Centre. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas, such as mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened its work on responsible investment for the Exchange Fund, particularly by setting a target for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced our risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. Moreover, to fully capture the potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment of the Exchange Fund, seeking investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation to enhance the portfolio’s long-term returns. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to the 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently been lower than the overall market. Going forward, we will continue to move towards the net-zero target by further integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, maintaining ongoing engagement with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Institutional Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility. On the environment front, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and advocating a more environmentally friendly market to the public. On the employee front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment. On the social responsibility front, we are dedicated to enhancing public financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to the community. Compared to the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development requires sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this critical global issue, we understand the need to lead by example and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section will outline the HKMA’s short-term plans and priorities in addressing climate change across its core functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will dedicate ourselves to reaching this goal. We are confident that, with the collective efforts of our colleagues, the financial industry, and the public, we can successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive, Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will work to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing climate risk management regulatory requirements, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector's "green benchmark". At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring different measures and technical solutions to help banks identify, calculate and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regulator-led regular stress tests for 2023-2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risks under an enhanced stress test framework, which covers various stress scenarios including extreme weather and adverse economic conditions. To promote the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide timely guidance on the sales process. We will also conduct off-site Box assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. At the same time, to strengthen the construction of a green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of developing a local green taxonomy framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broaden the scope of the programme to cover sustainable bonds; while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the government-funded Pilot Programme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training to expand Hong Kong's green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other institutional departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Commercial Banking Alliance, the HKMA will jointly launch various special initiatives with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the launch of project initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to participate in global climate action and implement the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the HKMA cares about its employees, the public and the surrounding environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to participate in global carbon reduction and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon emission reduction and encourage employees to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide further guidance to employees to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency, while minimising potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face the impact of various sustainability and climate-related matters in their daily business operations. To continue playing their important role in the financial system and channel more funds into green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the banking regulator, the HKMA is particularly focused on building banks' capacity to address and manage climate risk, and accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and has participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife smuggling. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)¹ published principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers these risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue to work on incorporating climate-related factors into its regulatory framework. Following the issuance of Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks, exchanging views on expectations, progress, and challenges in implementing relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, which was communicated to the banking industry in June. As part of implementing the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Framework" and enhanced the CAMEL² rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, the HKMA improved the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework based on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot exercise. The HKMA also formulated plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into the regular supervisory-led stress tests, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking industry's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Concurrently, the HKMA is reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, aiming to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks related to climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the increasing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing on banks' development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified some good practices during the thematic review and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, enabling banks to gradually strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks' ability to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risk on real estate. Additionally, the HKMA, together with other central banks and supervisory authorities, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network, exploring how technological solutions can assist in physical risk assessment. The HKMA also places great importance on promoting sustainable and leading global anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and compliance technology, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the manual burden and paper usage of banks. To enhance transparency among financial markets and align green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. A green classification framework, commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders, delving into the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and consult on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA recognises that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and therefore incorporates a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial vulnerability analysis and research to strengthen current monitoring efforts. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analysis of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisory authorities to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022, delving into two major topics: greenwashing³ in the corporate green bond market, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures⁴. The results of these studies help inform policy and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research seminars and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a secured backup funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the inclusion of sustainability considerations in the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and promoting sustainable finance as a mainstream issue. Through this participation, the HKMA helps facilitate policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability at the international and regional levels, and draws lessons to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To reinforce Hong Kong’s status as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and drivers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial industry’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy¹. The Steering Group’s work is primarily based on its strategic plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action agendas to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Diagram 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management and reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre. Promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection. Enhance the relevant skills of industry practitioners and raise public awareness and concern. Encourage product innovation and research initiatives to channel capital flows into green and sustainable projects. Seize opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area). Strengthen regional and international cooperation. Actions taken to date to advance Hong Kong’s sustainable finance development: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The current work priorities of the Steering Group include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see “Establishing a green classification framework to facilitate green capital flows” in the chapter “Building a sustainable financial system” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, in March, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong’s carbon market opportunities and will support Hong Kong’s development into a regional carbon trading hub, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and seizing opportunities from Greater Bay Area collaboration. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP² to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) was developed, facilitating companies’ sustainability reporting and helping financial institutions collect and analyse company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This is a significant step by the Steering Group to expand the coverage of its data work to include SMEs, a previously hard-to-reach yet important segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, and to build resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three information repositories on data, training information and internship opportunities, respectively, to help the financial industry and other sectors access green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support industry talent development, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Programme” in December, providing subsidies for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and upskilling. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the HKMA’s “Banking Professional Qualifications Framework” for banking practitioners³. “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Programme”. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”⁴, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential, mainstream green finance as a core business, and promote the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. It operates by providing a one-stop mutual learning platform for financial institutions to acquire the knowledge, tools and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions. It brings together green finance leaders, connects green financial institutions across different emerging markets, facilitates communication and explores frontier issues, and advances the global green finance agenda, unlocking endless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five globally leading financial institutions⁵ became founding members of the Alliance and work closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices in green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities, contributing to the green economic transition. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner⁶ committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas such as innovation, standardisation and academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Founding Members. The IFC and the HKMA signed a Memorandum of Understanding. Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtable meetings, attracting over 6,000 participants from around the world, including Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (Research Institute)⁷, published its first frontier research report entitled “Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation”. The HKMA has been promoting green and sustainable debt issuance and building a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to tackling climate change, promoting green finance and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued nearly US$16 billion equivalent in green institutional and retail bonds, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report”, detailing the allocation of proceeds from green bond issuances and the expected environmental benefits. To enable the public to participate in and share the outcomes of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the first batch of HK$20 billion in green retail bonds was issued in May, receiving strong public support and becoming the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, reinforcing its status as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance in the 2022-23 financial year, issuing US$5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency offering, covering US dollars, euros and renminbi with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continues to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in previous government green bond issuances, reflecting investor confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance amount of renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating in the issuance through the southbound Bond Connect also increased, showcasing Hong Kong as a premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond in February 2023 to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was one of the first tokenised green bonds issued by a government globally. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlement and maturity redemption) also digitised. This government issuance experience can serve as a reference for market participants interested in similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) to publish annual reports on the green debt market in Hong Kong and the region. ICMA’s report showed that in 2022, Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances, with a total of US$27.8 billion in bonds arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. The largest arranging hub for international green and sustainable bonds in Asia: US$27.8 billion. Following its first issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion in green and blue bonds⁸. In the same month, the People’s Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB5 billion in offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuance activities once again highlight Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” launched in 2021, using the Scheme to attract more related professional service providers (including financial institutions, green consultants and external reviewers) to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review service expenses of over 180 green and sustainable debt instrument issuers, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan amount threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises access green financing. Following the successful proof of concept for a tokenised retail green bond under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitising carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitised MOIs.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays a significant role in promoting green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Adhering to the principle of "preservation of capital first, long-term growth", the HKMA invests prudently, believing that focusing on ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value and mitigate related risks for investments. Facing the increasingly severe challenges of climate change, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "net-zero emissions by 2050" target in 2022 and optimising risk management strategies to enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio, thereby striving for better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulatory bodies to promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information is crucial for managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is to allow the HKMA to prioritise ESG investments with risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other projects, in line with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for monitoring the ESG and climate-related risks involved in Exchange Fund investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG profile of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Diagram 1, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and monitoring the ESG work of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions and work progress discussed at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Monitoring and governance structure of responsible investment A dedicated team within the Risk Management and Monitoring Division works closely with the investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across various investment categories: Public Market Investments The Credit, Regulation and Monitoring Committee, composed of senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of the fixed-income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Monitoring Division participates in the selection, appointment and monitoring process of external investment managers for equity portfolios from an ESG perspective (see the section "Proactive Stewardship" under "Risk Management" on page 27). Private Market Investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Monitoring Division and the private market investment teams for each investment proposal. Specific evidence² continues to show the significant impact of climate change and related risks. According to the latest report of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)³, even assuming the full implementation of the "Nationally Determined Contributions" targets announced by various regions, the estimated global temperature rise by 2100 could still be as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting the global average temperature increase to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, coupled with the repricing of asset valuation by markets based on expected future trends, along with inherent physical risks, will exacerbate pressure on asset valuations. In light of updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA, leveraging the expertise of external consultants, further assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund's "Investment Portfolio" under a "rapid transition" scenario (Diagram 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors in the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly lead to a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are abruptly divested to keep the average temperature rise within 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. This scenario is broadly consistent with the disorderly scenarios recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "Investment Portfolio" remains resilient in the medium to long term, as a larger proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may impact performance, particularly for equity assets, in the short term. The "Investment Portfolio" as a whole will face increasing impacts from physical risks that gradually manifest over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenario analysis, like other model-based methods, has its limitations. The analysis is based on the market benchmark sector distribution at the strategic asset allocation level and does not consider the effect of actively selecting specific securities within a sector. Deeper research shows that investments within the "Investment Portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or suffer less impact compared to the market benchmark of the strategic asset allocation. This result reaffirms that the HKMA's responsible investment, focused on combating climate change, can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve with improvements in data quality and policy developments. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and optimise assessments to more clearly confirm the Exchange Fund's resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change can bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities related to climate transition, mitigating climate risks, and enhancing the long-term returns of the asset portfolio. In 2022, the HKMA continued its good momentum, increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by another 50%. In equity investments, the HKMA invests in governance-themed active equity portfolios and adopts a decarbonisation strategy for passive equity portfolios that favours companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Diagram 3). Diagram 3: Continued implementation of measures to increase ESG investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator, which, in addition to producing clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity factors. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poison baits to prevent predatory animals from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that are endangered. Livestock are important assets for local villagers. To help villagers protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect them from natural predators. Additionally, the operator employs bird monitors to issue warnings when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left by predators, so that the wind turbines can be shut down to prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: it safeguards the livelihoods of the villagers while reducing the number of vultures killed by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operation. The investee company is an integrated logistics warehousing operator in Mainland China, specialising in cold chain pharmaceuticals, chemical products and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operational standards, mainly driven by multinational corporate clients requiring its service providers to meet high decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to this demand, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "three-year ESG plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan had already yielded significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company the "Low Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. These achievements and recognitions have enabled the company to secure numerous business opportunities from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that particularly value ESG practices. The growth of ESG investments is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its 4th annual ESG Workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions (including dedicated partners, limited partners and corporates), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public markets, the HKMA urged its trading partners (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr. LEE Tat-chi, Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered the opening address at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in formulating industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participates in the signatory joint action coordinated by the PRI to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire for private equity and venture capital investments⁵, ⁶, to assist private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in several working groups to support the research work of FCLTGlobal; this research aims to explore market best practices for long-term investment portfolios and decarbonising private assets, and the application of these practices to long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS's "Climate-related Disclosures for Central Banks" guidance, demonstrating its commitment to adopting good ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a working group under the NGFS's "Net Zero for Central Banks" workstream, participating in the formulation of sustainable and responsible investment approaches for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. LAU Wai-kuen, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (centre), speaking at an ESG investment opportunity sharing session Building internal capacity is crucial for continuing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to take relevant courses and obtain relevant qualifications in sustainable development, the HKMA has also gained knowledge and practical experience from the advice provided by external consultants in 2021 on key industry practices for portfolio climate transition. Furthermore, the HKMA utilises ESG data compiled by reputable external information providers to supplement its ongoing analysis of the asset portfolio, thereby helping to strengthen the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, and contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate targets. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also fulfils its commitments to caring for staff well-being, encouraging financial inclusion, and fulfilling social responsibilities. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA practises the concept of sustainable development under three pillars: environment, staff, and social responsibility (Diagram 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee leads the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. Chaired by the HKMA Chief Executive, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk Management and Surveillance Division and the Corporate Development and Operations Division, and reports regularly to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of this Committee, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures in their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved the climate targets for the HKMA's operations and reviewed the transition roadmap towards achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review progress on the HKMA's green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen the HKMA's sustainable procurement policy, procedures, and methods. Governance structure for sustainability The HKMA's institutional sustainability journey In recognition of the HKMA's commitment to caring for the environment, staff, and the community at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the "15 Years Plus Caring Company" logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to its own carbon footprint and has formulated internal "Green Office Guidelines" to control the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has integrated environmental considerations into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the HKMA was awarded a Gold rating under BEAM Plus for certain renovated office areas. This is the second green building certification obtained by the HKMA, following the LEED Gold certification awarded in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interiors Version 1.0 Gold rating The HKMA implements various energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 6 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per person 7 ), a decrease of 24.4% compared to 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 8 were 2,996.4 tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per person), a decrease of 38.2% compared to 2015 (Figure 2). Figure 1 Figure 2 Greenhouse gas emission intensity (Scope 1 and 2) The HKMA encourages paperless operations within the institution. Additionally, the HKMA implements a print management system requiring staff to log in to the printer to confirm each print job, helping to reduce unnecessary printouts and toner usage. Where printing is necessary, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic records management system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per person), a decrease of 65.3% compared to 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: Paper consumption intensity The HKMA's waste management continues to follow the "4R" principle. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA also reduces electronic waste by adopting technical solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit, analysing the composition of waste generated in the office. The audit found that food waste constituted a significant portion of total waste, leading the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see page 41 "Enhancing waste management"). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general refuse and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per person), a decrease of 4.8% compared to 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuations were mainly due to work-from-home arrangements during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave. Figure 3 Non-hazardous waste intensity The HKMA prioritises waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to better understand the composition of waste in daily operations (plastics, paper, metal, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) and to provide recommendations for waste reduction. Based on the audit results, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, placing food waste collection bins in all pantries. The food waste collected daily is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy for power generation. The residues from the conversion process can also be made into compost for landscaping and agricultural use. In addition, recycling bins are placed in various locations in the office for easy use. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays more attention to further improving the source separation of recyclables, as well as the handling of recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles.
